front: Trap — d12 / d12-q25: what's wrong with this instinct?

front: Trap — d12 / d12-q26: what's wrong with this instinct?

front: Trap — d12 / d12-q27: what's wrong with this instinct?

front: Trap — d12 / d12-q28: what's wrong with this instinct?

front: Walk through the end-to-end architecture of a document intelligence RAG platform from ingest to generate. Who owns what between NestJS and FastAPI?

front: How would you design semantic chunking and metadata for planning PDFs on a document intelligence RAG platform?

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q03: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Fixed 500-token windows through tables — splits numbers from labels and tanks answer quality.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q04: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Vector-only across a shared index — tenancy becomes a prompt instruction, which is not an access control.

front: How do you make LLM calls production-grade with structured outputs, versioned prompts, bounded retries, and typed errors?

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q05: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: json.loads on free-form model text with no schema — one extra trailing comma poisons an entire document version.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q06: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Generating a new UUID inside the worker per attempt — every retry looks like new work and doubles embeddings.

front: Design org-scoped multi-tenancy and HMAC authentication between NestJS and FastAPI. What isolation failure modes matter most?
back: Tenancy is enforced in signatures and storage keys, not in prompts. HMAC proves Nest called us; org-scoped indexes and caches prove we cannot leak across customers.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q07: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Passing org_id only in the JSON body without signing — attackers who reach the worker pick any tenant.

front: How do you design S3 handoff between NestJS and FastAPI with compensating cleanup when the downstream stage fails?

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q08: what's wrong with this instinct?

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q09: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Letting any service push breaking schema without composition checks — clients fail in production first.

front: How do you keep Elasticsearch course search consistent with Mongo as the source of truth on an institutional LMS?

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q10: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Dual-writing ES inside the HTTP handler — ES downtime blocks course administration.

front: Design WebSocket chat for 1000+ concurrent users on an institutional LMS: persistence, reliable delivery, and fan-out/backpressure.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q11: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Fan-out before durable write — acknowledged UI messages disappear on crash.

front: Mongo activity collection is ~16M documents / ~160GB. How would you design a live vs archive split?

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q12: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Deleting from live before archive durability is proven — unrecoverable learner history loss.

front: You claim ~71% working-set reduction with zero learner-metric delta. How do you prove safety before and after cutover?

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q13: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Using only disk metrics as success — learners can break while Grafana looks green on GB.

front: Why would you reject a compaction that risks ~21K enrolments for roughly ~0.3% storage savings?
back: I reject asymmetric bets: ~0.3% savings versus ~21K enrolments is not engineering thrift—it is negligence. We take storage wins that do not wager the enrolment graph.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q14: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Optimising for storage dashboards while ignoring learner-state blast radius — wrong objective function.

front: Design data-lifecycle operations for the institutional LMS: distributed locks, run ledgers, dry-run and restore probes.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q15: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Cron without a lock — two pods prune the same window and race deletes.

front: Where would you put Redis on hot GraphQL paths in an institutional LMS—what to cache, how to invalidate, how to stop stampedes?
back: Cache shared, authz-safe projections with org-aware keys. Invalidate on write, jitter TTLs, and single-flight misses so Redis speeds GraphQL without becoming a consistency or stampede bomb.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q16: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Caching GraphQL responses without authz in the key — cross-learner data leaks.

front: How would you structure a healthcare diagnostics platform with modular DDD on FastAPI (patient, appointment, records, billing)?
back: Modular DDD keeps clinical and billing languages apart. FastAPI packages own their invariants and talk through APIs/events—not shared tables—so the healthcare diagnostics platform can evolve safely.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q17: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: One giant models.py for all contexts — boundaries exist only on slides.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q18: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Big-bang DNS cutover without shadow — first production day is your integration test.

back: Validate commands up front, enqueue durable work second, and treat DLQ as a paging signal. CQRS on Cloud Tasks/Pub/Sub only works if handlers are idempotent and lag is visible.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q19: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Enqueueing first and validating in the worker — the bus fills with garbage and clinical ops drown.

front: Design lab-result ingestion with GPT vision transcription: JSON validation, unit normalisation, and risk-based human review.
back: Vision proposes; validation and units constrain; risk policy decides what humans must see. Clinical safety beats end-to-end automation vanity metrics.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q20: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Writing raw model JSON to the patient record — schema drift becomes clinical data drift.

front: For HIPAA-aligned controls on a healthcare diagnostics platform (Firebase Auth, encryption, RBAC, audit), what do you actually verify in the design?

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q21: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Equating 'we use Firebase Auth' with HIPAA compliance — identity alone is not minimum-necessary access.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q22: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Adding every possible composite index — write amplification and deployment pain for unused paths.

back: Emulators for our data/auth boundaries, mocks for expensive probabilistic externals, coverage as a critical-path floor. That is how you approach ~92% without lying to yourself.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q23: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Mocking Firestore so thoroughly that security rules never run — false confidence on PHI access.

front: Give a cross-cutting production failure story framework (detect → mitigate → permanent fix) usable on the document intelligence RAG platform, institutional LMS, or healthcare diagnostics platform.
back: Detect with SLIs, mitigate to stop harm, then fix the system and prove it with alerts and a game-day. Same framework whether the blast is RAG retrieval, LMS data lifecycle, or clinical projections.

front: Trap — d13 / d13-q24: what's wrong with this instinct?
back: Jumping to root-cause debates while blast radius grows — patients/learners keep getting hurt during the argument.

front: Story probe — Biggest owned project: What did YOU personally decide? What went wrong? What measurable outcome?
back: Lead with your decisions and tradeoffs, not 'the team'. Name risks you owned, one failure, and a metric (latency, cost, adoption, error rate) that moved.

front: Story probe — Difficult technical decision: Alternatives? Rejected why? Evidence? Would you choose the same today?
back: List ≥2 real alternatives, rejection criteria, and whether the decision was reversible. Update with hindsight without rewriting history.

front: Story probe — Missed deadline: When did you know it was at risk? When did you tell stakeholders? What did you change?
back: Early risk beat late apology. Include what you cut, who you aligned, and the new date you defended.

front: Story probe — Mentoring: Baseline → what you changed → evidence of growth.
back: Avoid 'I answered their questions.' Cite task sizing, review habits, independence metrics (PRs merged without rescue).

front: Story probe — Disagreement: What was the conflict? Your evidence? What happened after the decision?
back: Show challenge without ego, data or scenarios used, and either commit or escalate with documented risk.

front: Story probe — Production incident: Detect → your actions → mitigate → permanent change.
back: Own mitigation and comms first; RCA second. End with a preventive change (alert, test, runbook, guardrail).

front: Story probe — Technical debt: Why accept? Cost? When repaid?
back: Name the invariant you refused to break, the shortcut taken, the repayment ticket/date, and whether it actually got paid.

front: Story probe — Unclear requirements: Ambiguity identified → how reduced → what shipped.
back: Show written assumptions, thin confirmed slice, and what you deferred on purpose.

front: Story probe — Failure: Your personal mistake → what you changed afterward.
back: Use 'I' not 'we'. Immediate mitigation, honest comms, and a systemic fix so it cannot recur the same way.

front: Story probe — Improvement: How identified → why it mattered → measurable impact.
back: Tie to user/business or reliability cost. Prefer before/after numbers over activity narratives.

front: Senior vs mid — Implementing a feature vs owning a feature?
back: Implement = code merges. Own = contracts, risks, rollout, metrics, and post-launch health until outcomes land.

front: Senior vs mid — Fixing a prod issue vs improving the system that allowed it?
back: Fix restores service. Improve adds detection, prevention, and ownership so the class of failure shrinks.

front: Senior vs mid — Delegating work vs developing engineers?
back: Delegate assigns tasks. Develop sizes growth, reviews design early, and measures independence—not permanent dependence.

front: Senior vs mid — Making a technical decision vs driving one?
back: Making picks an option. Driving aligns stakeholders, records rationale, and lands the decision in code and ops.

front: Senior vs mid — Communicating status vs communicating project risk?
back: Status is progress. Risk names likelihood, impact, options, and the decision you need now.

front: Senior vs mid — Writing good code vs maintaining a healthy service?
back: Good code is local quality. Healthy service means SLOs, alerts, runbooks, and operable failure modes.

front: Senior vs mid — Technically correct vs good engineering decision?
back: Correct can still be wrong for time, cost, risk, or reversibility. Good decisions optimize outcomes under constraints.

front: Senior vs mid — Solving a ticket vs solving the underlying problem?
back: Ticket closes a symptom. Underlying problem removes the class of defects or process that generates them.

front: Senior vs mid — Being busy vs creating engineering impact?
back: Busy fills the calendar. Impact moves a metric users or the business feel—or a risk that would have hurt them.

front: Senior vs mid — Owning implementation vs owning outcomes?
back: Implementation ownership ends at merge. Outcome ownership includes production behavior, adoption, and follow-through.
